'''David S. Slepian''' (June 30, 1923 &ndash; November 29, 2007) was an American [[mathematician]]. He is best known for his work with [[algebraic coding theory]], [[probability theory]], and [[distributed source coding]]. He was colleagues with [[Claude Shannon]] and [[Richard Hamming]] at [[Bell Labs]].

==Life and work==
Born in [[Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania]], he gained a [[B.Sc.]] at [[University of Michigan]] before joining the US Army in [[World War II]], 
as a [[sonic deception]] officer in the 3133rd Signal Service Company of the [[Ghost Army]].<ref>{{cite web |title=David Slepian |url=https://ghostarmy.org/roster/David-Slepian/ |website=The Ghost Army Legacy Project |access-date=1 January 2026}}</ref>

He received his [[Ph.D.]] from [[Harvard University]] in 1949, writing his dissertation in physics. After post-doctoral work at the 
[[University of Cambridge]] and [[University of Sorbonne]], he worked at the Mathematics Research Center at [[Bell Labs|Bell Telephone Laboratories]], where he pioneered work in [[algebraic coding theory]] on [[group code]]s, first published in the paper ''A Class of Binary Signaling Alphabets''. Here, he also worked along with other information theory giants such as [[Claude Shannon]] and [[Richard Hamming]]. He also proved the possibility of [[singular detection]], a perhaps unintuitive result. He is also known for [[Slepian's lemma]] in [[probability theory]] (1962), and for discovering a fundamental result in
[[distributed source coding]] called [[Slepian–Wolf coding]] with [[Jack Keil Wolf]] (1973).

He later joined the [[University of Hawaiʻi]]. His father was [[Joseph Slepian]], also a scientist.<ref name="IEEE-DavidSlepian">{{cite web|url=http://www.ieeeghn.org/wiki/index.php/David_Slepian |title=IEEE Global History Network - David Slepian |publisher=[[IEEE]] |access-date=February 22, 2011}}</ref> His wife is the noted children's author [[Jan Slepian]].

==Slepian Functions==
[[File:DPSS figure.svg|thumb|Three examples of [[Slepian function|Slepian functions]], named after David Slepian.]]

Slepian's joint work with H.J. Landau and H.O. Pollak<ref name="BSTJ-DPSWF1">{{cite web|url=http://www.alcatel-lucent.com/bstj/vol40-1961/articles/bstj40-1-43.pdf | title=Prolate Spheroidal Wave Functions, Fourier Analysis and Uncertainty -- I | publisher=[[BSTJ]] | access-date=June 15, 2012}}</ref><ref name="BSTJ-DPSWF2">{{cite web|url=http://www.alcatel-lucent.com/bstj/vol40-1961/articles/bstj40-1-65.pdf | title=Prolate Spheroidal Wave Functions, Fourier Analysis and Uncertainty -- II | publisher=[[BSTJ]] | access-date=June 15, 2012}}</ref><ref name="BSTJ-DPSWF3">{{cite web|url=http://www.alcatel-lucent.com/bstj/vol41-1962/articles/bstj41-4-1295.pdf | title=Prolate Spheroidal Wave Functions, Fourier Analysis and Uncertainty -- III: The Dimension of the Space of Essentially Time- and Band-Limited Signals | publisher=[[BSTJ]] | access-date=June 15, 2012}}</ref><ref name="BSTJ-DPSWF4">{{cite web|url=http://www.alcatel-lucent.com/bstj/vol43-1964/articles/bstj43-6-3009.pdf | title=Prolate Spheroidal Wave Functions, Fourier Analysis and Uncertainty -- IV: Extensions to Many Dimensions; Generalized Prolate Spheroidal Functions | publisher=[[BSTJ]] | access-date=June 15, 2012}}</ref><ref name="BSTJ-DPSWF5">{{cite web|url=http://www.alcatel-lucent.com/bstj/vol57-1978/articles/bstj57-5-1371.pdf | title=Prolate Spheroidal Wave Functions, Fourier Analysis and Uncertainty -- V: The Discrete Case | publisher=[[BSTJ]] | access-date=June 15, 2012}}</ref> on discrete prolate spheroidal wave functions and sequences (DPSWF, DPSS) eventually led to the naming of the sequences as [[Slepian function|Slepian functions]] or "Slepians". The naming suggestion was provided by [[Robert Ladislav Parker|Bob Parker]] of Scripp's Institute of Oceanography, who suggested that "discrete prolate spheroidal sequences" was a "mouthful". The term "prolates" is equally in current use.

This work was fundamental to the development of the method of [[multitaper]] spectral analysis, where the discrete Slepian functions are used as an essential component to provide [[bias]] control while reducing estimation [[variance]].
